title: Lifelong Maintenance

learn.summary: Languages are use-it-or-lose-it: attrition research shows unused skills decay measurably within months, with speaking fading before comprehension. The good news is maintenance is cheap — a few engaged hours weekly holds a B2, and re-activation is far faster than first learning. Past the exam-and-milestone phase, the language stops being a project and becomes a channel: friends, books, films, places.

do: Write your maintenance plan on one line: the minimum weekly dose (e.g. one conversation plus two hours of media) you will not go below.

children.title: The Maintenance Dose

learn.summary: Maintenance differs from learning: you no longer need new material daily, you need regular activation of what you have — especially speaking, the most perishable skill. A workable floor is one real conversation plus a couple of hours of native media per week, anchored to existing habits so it survives busy seasons. Passive-only maintenance (just watching shows) preserves comprehension but lets your speaking quietly rust.

do: Put a recurring weekly conversation (tutor, tandem, or friend) in your calendar as a permanent standing appointment.

children.title: Fighting Attrition

learn.summary: First-language-style attrition hits second languages harder: retrieval slows, then production vocabulary shrinks, while reading survives longest. Monika Schmid's attrition research offers comfort, though — well-learned material is dormant, not deleted, and 'savings' effects mean relearning is dramatically faster than initial learning. If you lapse for a year, expect a rusty month, not a restart.

do: After any lapse of a month or more, run a one-week reactivation sprint: daily listening plus two booked conversations.

children.title: Adding Languages

learn.summary: Research on multilingualism shows third languages come faster: you already know how you learn, and related languages share vocabulary and structure. The trap is 'wanderlust' — starting language three before language two can survive on maintenance alone, which usually kills both. Rule of thumb: get the current language to a stable B2 before adding another, and expect interference (mixing) between close languages at first.

do: Before starting a new language, verify your current one passes the maintenance test: a comfortable 15-minute conversation after two weeks of no study.

children.title: Cultural Depth

learn.summary: Past B2, progress is mostly cultural: humor, politeness norms, register-switching, references everyone but you gets. Sociolinguistics — including phenomena like code-switching — shows that 'native-like' is less about grammar than about knowing which of five correct sentences a native would actually say. This is the permanently interesting part: films without subtitles, novels, arguments, friendships that run entirely in the language.

do: Pick one culturally iconic film or novel in your language this month and discuss it with a native speaker afterward.
